sample_query.user_prompt:
This person is a 27-year-old single mother in Detroit who works rotating night shifts in a fulfillment warehouse, and she wants universal free childcare from birth to include guaranteed infant slots reserved during pregnancy, 24/7 coverage including weekends and overnights, sibling priority, and a single multilingual online portal that verifies eligibility without long office visits because she has repeatedly lost hours and pay when care fell through. I lost a week’s pay when my infant’s spot vanished after maternity leave, so being able to reserve a slot during pregnancy matters most to me. I was written up after two no-shows when my backup sitter canceled at 1 a.m., so reliable 24/7 coverage isn’t optional for me. A single online portal where I can upload documents from my phone would save me two bus rides and half a day of unpaid wait time every time paperwork needs renewing. Without true 24/7 coverage, including overnights and weekends, one more attendance write-up could cost me my job and health insurance.

They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: "Should the government provide universal free childcare from birth?"

OPINION STATEMENT:
The group of participants believe that free childcare from birth should be made available to all children as it will be better for both the parents and the children. Childcare costs are very high, and many people cannot afford them. If they were free, many parents could take up employment, allowing them to provide for their families. This would also mean that the government would be receiving more money from taxes, which would help fund the country. The children will also benefit from free childcare as they will get to interact with other children and learn from them. They will be in a safer environment, being looked after by qualified professionals. The government should ensure that all children are looked after to a high standard.

They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:

POLICY PROPOSAL:
Universal free childcare from birth: 30 hours/week for 0–12 months (voluntary, infant-specific staffing ratios, health visitor integration) rising to 40 hours/week for ages 1–5, with a regulated option for home-based carers; funded by consolidating existing subsidies and a 1% VAT rise; maximizes access from day one but is high-cost and contingent on recruiting sufficient carers.

After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.
Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?

prompt_construction:
def prompt_fn(*, rater:str, policy:str, case:str, scenario_params:dict, instruct_tuned:bool=False) -> list[str]:
    base_context = (
        f"{rater}\n\n"
        f"They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: \"{scenario_params['question']}\"\n\n"
        f"OPINION STATEMENT:\n{policy}\n\n"
        f"They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:\n\n"
        f"POLICY PROPOSAL:\n{case}\n\n"
        "After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.\n"
    )

    prompt1 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    prompt2 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal contradict/stand in opposition to the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    if instruct_tuned:
        return [prompt1, prompt2]

    prompts = [prompt1, prompt2]
    prompts = [p + "\nAnswer:" for p in prompts]
    return prompts

cases: Universal free childcare from birth: 30 hours/week for 0–12 months (voluntary, infant-specific staffing ratios, health visitor integration) rising to 40 hours/week for ages 1–5, with a regulated option for home-based carers; funded by consolidating existing subsidies and a 1% VAT rise; maximizes access from day one but is high-cost and contingent on recruiting sufficient carers.

Merit: supports infant bonding and early learning while phasing public costs; tradeoff: slower return to full-time work in the first half-year.

Work-Linked Targeted Childcare: Free childcare from birth to school entry for single parents and households below 60% of median income, and for any parent in employment, job search, or accredited training up to 35 hours per week; others pay a sliding co-pay capped at 7% of household income. Eligibility is verified via HMRC Real Time Information and Universal Credit records; funded by consolidating existing childcare subsidies and a 0.5% payroll levy on employers with over 250 employees. Merits: focuses resources on need and supports work; Costs: administrative complexity and co-pays for middle- and high-income families.

Employer-Shared Childcare with Non-Parent Offset: Employers with 100+ staff must provide on-site or contracted childcare places equal to 5% of headcount or pay 1% of payroll into a National Childcare Fund; the fund, topped up by general revenue, delivers universal free care from birth to age 2 up to 30 hours per week. Adult taxpayers without dependent children receive a £400 annual tax rebate or lifelong learning credit; providers get grants for quality improvement and Level 3 childcare apprenticeships. Merits: spreads costs between employers and government and addresses fairness concerns; Costs: increased employer costs and public expenditure.

The government establishes a Universal Free Childcare Guarantee from birth to school entry: up to 40 hours/week free care in a mixed public-private system, with a national caregiver wage floor, compulsory staff-child ratios, and paid apprenticeships to expand the workforce; capital grants fund new centers near transit and employers; financed by a 1% surtax on incomes over $300,000 and a levy on share buybacks. High upfront fiscal cost and staffing pressures are offset by higher parental labor force participation and long-run productivity.

A Targeted Childcare Voucher and Employer Duty: means-tested vouchers covering 100% of childcare fees for children 6-36 months in households below median income (phasing down to 50% at 250% of median), conditional on a parent working or enrolled in training; 30 hours/week standard with extended hours for shift workers; firms with 250+ employees must provide on-site care or contribute 0.5% payroll to a childcare fund. Lower cost than universal but excludes non-working parents and may create cliff effects.

Care-at-Home Allowance with Extended, Well-Paid Parental Leave: A tax-free GBP 400 per month per child allowance for families with children under 3 who use fewer than 10 hours per week of state-funded childcare, alongside 18 months of shared parental leave at 80 percent wage replacement (capped), a legal right to part-time or remote work in the first year, and strong job protection. Funded by consolidating current childcare tax credits and a small employer payroll levy. Tradeoffs: supports parent-led care and infant bonding but reduces short-term labor supply and adds employer compliance costs.

Two-Child Free Childcare Cap plus Secular and Continuity Standards: Free childcare from birth is provided for a household’s first two children; additional children receive a tapered, means-tested subsidy. Families may opt for an equivalent home-care credit instead of institutional care. Participating providers must assign a primary keyworker per infant, meet enhanced infant-care training certification, and provide a secular, non-proselytizing environment. Financed by a 0.5 percentage point VAT rise earmarked for early years. Rationale: limits fiscal exposure and avoids pronatalist incentives; Downside: non-universal per-child access and potential equity concerns for larger families.

Childcare Choice Guarantee from birth to age 3: every child is entitled either to a free full-time childcare place (no caps) or a tax-free monthly Care Allowance of equal value for parents who provide care at home or use informal carers; entitlements are portable and switchable monthly, with part‑time options; includes home‑visiting early‑years support; providers reimbursed at cost‑plus rates tied to quality benchmarks; funded from general taxation with attendance verification and audits to limit misuse.

Universal free childcare from 9 months until school start (up to 40 hours/week), delivered through a mixed public–private network paid at parity rates, paired with 9 months paid parental leave from birth (first 6 months at 90% wage replacement, remaining 3 months at flat-rate) to protect early bonding; national workforce plan sets a living-wage pay floor, funded training, and faster site licensing; financed by a 1% employer payroll levy plus general taxation; phased in over 3 years to manage cost and staffing.

Employer Childcare Obligation or Levy: Require employers with 250 or more staff to either provide on-site or contracted childcare places equal to 5% of headcount, or pay a £600 per employee annual levy into a local childcare expansion fund; offer SMEs a 150% tax deduction for contributions to shared childcare hubs; include a right to predictable schedules for parents of children under 3 and fund provider training through levy receipts. Tradeoff: higher taxes and short-term capacity constraints during expansion.

Employer Childcare Partnership and Scheduling Act: Require employers with 50+ workers to provide one of (a) guaranteed on-site or contracted childcare slots, (b) a monthly childcare benefit of at least $500 per eligible child, or (c) contributions to a portable childcare benefit account; the federal government matches 50% of benefit costs for firms under 250 employees and funds extended-hours micro-centers for shift workers; include a right-to-request predictable schedules. Fund matches by trimming low-value business tax expenditures. Tradeoff: expands access tied to employment and reduces direct public spend, but raises employer costs and may exclude non-employed caregivers.

Targeted Free Care + Affordability Cap: From birth to school entry, childcare is free for households under 200% of the federal poverty line when a parent is working, in education, or seeking work 20+ hours/week; for others, co-pays are capped at 7% of household income on a sliding scale. Fund via consolidating existing childcare subsidies and a 0.3% payroll surtax on wages above the Social Security cap; expand supply with grants to providers meeting quality and wage standards. Tradeoff: reduces child poverty and boosts parental employment but adds payroll costs and administrative means-testing.

Universal Free Childcare from 6 Months: Provide 30 hours/week of free, high-quality childcare for all children from 6 months until school entry, delivered through a mixed public/voluntary/private network; fund via a surtax on top incomes and repurposing existing fragmented subsidies; launch a National Early Years Workforce Plan (tuition-free training, paid apprenticeships, immigration fast-track, wage floor linked to teacher starting pay), capital grants to expand nurseries, and enforce improved staff-child ratios; phase in by age cohort over 4 years. Tradeoffs: large fiscal cost and rapid workforce expansion required, offset by higher labor force participation and long-run child development gains.

Targeted Childcare Guarantee with Sliding Co-pays: Guarantee up to 35 hours/week of free childcare for households below 60% of median income (or on specified benefits) from 9 months to school entry; above that threshold, introduce income-based co-pays capped at 7% of household income; include a refundable tax credit for part-time or informal care and an optional home-care stipend for parents of 0-12-month infants; eligibility tied to work, education, or active job search; pay higher provider rates and quality bonuses in disadvantaged areas. Phase in a 'First 1,000 Days' guarantee: months 0–12 covered by paid parental leave at 80% of earnings (funded by a 0.6% employee and 0.6% employer social insurance contribution), months 13–36 guaranteed 30 hours/week free early education and care, with additional hours income-tested; launch a national early-years workforce plan (tuition-free apprenticeships, £5,000 bursaries, fast-track visas) and rural micro-centre grants to expand supply; trade-off: higher payroll costs for employers and near-term service shortages as the workforce scales.

Create a targeted Childcare Affordability Credit that caps out-of-pocket childcare costs at 7% of household income for families up to 150% of median income, delivered as a monthly refundable credit or direct-to-provider voucher; pair with a 50% tax credit (up to £6,000 per seat) for employers that provide on-site childcare or reserve contracted places, plus portable childcare benefits for shift workers; fund by consolidating existing childcare entitlements and phasing out higher-earner childcare tax reliefs; trade-off: families above the threshold do not receive free care and coverage may vary where employer participation is low.

The government provides universal free childcare from 6 months to school start for 40 hours/week at accredited providers, paired with a 5-year £8bn capacity program (nursery capital grants, a £13/hour wage floor, and 40,000 training bursaries) and national per-child rates; funded by a 1% National Insurance surcharge on earnings above £75,000 and ending higher-rate childcare voucher relief; boosts labor supply and gender equity but requires higher taxation and rapid workforce expansion.

A universal base of 20 free hours/week from 9 months is provided to all children, with an additional 20 hours for parents in work or education; employers with 250+ staff must provide on-site places for 3% of their workforce's children or pay a 0.4% payroll levy to local childcare trusts; levy revenues plus £2bn central co-funding finance provider wage uplifts, fast-track apprenticeships, and visas to recruit 50,000 early-years workers; shares costs across employers and the state and speeds capacity growth, but may raise employer costs and prices.

National Early Years Public Option (from 12 months): Universal 30 hours/week free childcare from 12 months to school entry delivered via a public-mixed network, with birth–11 months limited to targeted at-risk families; mandates key-worker continuity (one primary caregiver per child), low ratios (1:3 under-2s), secular evidence-based curriculum, and attachment-focused training; optional paid top-ups for additional hours; financed by a 0.3% employer payroll levy with NIC relief for low-wage firms. Justification: supports workforce participation and child development while containing costs by excluding the first year.

Targeted Childcare Affordability Guarantee for ages 0–3: Means-tested vouchers that cap net childcare fees at 7% of household income for families up to median income, paid directly to accredited providers meeting wage and quality standards; funded by tapering Tax-Free Childcare for the top two income deciles and restricting higher-rate pension tax relief. Justification: reduces costs for low- and middle-income families at lower fiscal cost than universal free care.

Launch a targeted Work‑Return Childcare Credit starting at 9 months with employer co‑funding: cover 85% of childcare fees up to £900 per month per child for working, job‑seeking, or training parents, delivered through PAYE or Universal Credit with a 15% family co‑pay; offer a 50% tax credit to employers (capped at £2,000 per worker annually) for on‑site creches, shift‑friendly hours, or direct childcare top‑ups; grant providers funds to extend hours to 6am–10pm in sectors with atypical shifts; maintain the existing universal 15 hours for ages 3–4 but add no new universal infant entitlement; lower fiscal cost and strong work incentives, but non‑working parents receive limited support.

Introduce a universal portable childcare entitlement from 6 months to school start delivered as a monthly voucher: auto‑load £1,000 per child (regionally indexed) into expanded Tax‑Free Childcare accounts, redeemable with any accredited provider including nurseries, childminders, co‑ops, and employer creches; allow families to top up above a national fee cap and do not require use of the entitlement; pair with transparent quality ratings and a provider price cap to limit inflation; fund by consolidating existing early‑years budgets and a 0.5% National Insurance rise; faster to implement and preserves parental choice, but risks supply gaps without targeted rural and infant‑care grants.

Introduce a universal core entitlement of 15 hours/week free childcare for ages 1–4, with means-tested top-ups to 30–40 hours for the bottom 40% of households and 50% subsidies for middle incomes; phase in by age cohort over three years; fund via capping higher-rate pension tax relief to 30% and a modest increase in sugar and tobacco duties; include a £1/hour provider wage uplift to prevent closures. Merit: broad access with cost controls; Trade-off: part-time coverage may not fit full-time work patterns.

Guarantee 35 hours/week free childcare from 6 months to school age for households below 60% of median income, with a smooth taper to a 30% co-pay up to the 90th percentile; above that, offer a refundable tax credit of 20% of fees up to £3,000 per child; add an optional £300/month home-care allowance for the first 12 months for parents who forgo publicly funded childcare; invest £500m in fast-track early-years workforce training tied to new places in deprived areas; fund by consolidating existing schemes and closing high-end childcare tax relief loopholes. Merit: targets poverty traps and workforce participation; Trade-off: increased means-testing complexity.

Universal Child Development Allowance from birth: $400/month per child paid to the default caregiver (mother unless the father elects), usable for any child-related expense; fully universal for the first child, with the allowance for second and subsequent children tapering between $100,000–$200,000 household income; no universal free childcare expansion, with targeted childcare fee subsidies retained only for low-income households. Increases flexibility and administrative simplicity; tradeoff: does not guarantee access to high-quality early education or lower market childcare prices.

Early Years Quality and Capacity Act (6–36 months): mandatory national standards for infant/toddler care (e.g., 1:3 staff-to-infant ratio, diploma-level training, developmental curriculum) paired with a five-year public workforce pipeline (tuition-free early-educator training, paid apprenticeships) and wage floors indexed to local K–12 pay; families receive a voucher from 6 months equal to the local median cost of 30 hours/week that is worth 20% more at top-rated providers or can be taken as a 70% value at-home care stipend. Raises quality and supply while preserving choice; tradeoff: higher provider costs and potential reduction of low-fee informal options.

Universal Care-Choice from Birth: Provide up to 30 hours/week free childcare for every child from birth to age 3 via a public option and accredited providers at a single national rate; families who prefer home care can take a tax-free Care-Choice Credit worth 70% of the subsidy plus home-visiting support; fund capital build-out and workforce training grants to expand supply; funded by a high-income surtax and redirecting existing childcare subsidies; merits: universal access without pressuring parents to work; costs: high fiscal and staffing demands in early years.

12+ Free Childcare with Regional Childcare Trusts: Guarantee 35 hours/week free childcare from 12 months to school entry for all families; create regional publicly commissioned trusts that franchise providers on 10-year contracts, set staff pay floors and training standards, and run a single enrollment system to replace the fragmented market; infants under 12 months receive means-tested hours only; funded by general taxation plus a 0.3% payroll levy on large employers; merits: reduces cost and chaos and speeds parental return to work; tradeoffs: transition could force consolidation and temporarily reduce local choice.

Universal Family Starter Package: 12 months paid parental leave per child (6 months reserved for each parent, 80% wage replacement up to the median wage, self-employed included), plus universal free childcare from 6 to 60 months in licensed settings; parents may convert months 6 to 12 of leave into free childcare hours (for example, 30 hours per week) or take the cash leave instead; funded by a 0.8% payroll levy split employer and employee and general revenue; quality standards require developmental curricula and staff-to-child ratios; tradeoff: higher tax levy and provider expansion costs in the first 3 years.

First-Year-at-Home Option: prohibit public funding of center-based care for infants younger than 12 months except for medical or hardship exemptions; instead provide a monthly, taxable infant care allowance of 1,200 dollars for the first 12 months, stackable with unpaid leave protections and part-time work rights; expand home-visiting and lactation support; create a small pool of emergency, 24-7 state-run infant care slots for essential workers; sunset review in 5 years; tradeoff: reduces early return-to-work options for some parents and may impact labor supply, but concentrates resources on parental care and infant health.

The government provides 12 months of paid parental leave at 80% wage replacement (capped at the median wage), with a non-transferable 3-month second-parent quota; upon return to work, parents receive a six-month $800/month flexible childcare voucher usable only with licensed providers, and employers with 50-plus staff must offer flexible schedules or on-site or contracted care (with a tax credit for small businesses). Merit: supports infant bonding and smoother re-entry to work while boosting licensed care demand; Tradeoff: payroll contribution increases and compliance burdens for employers.

The government enacts a universal Family Freedom Allowance from birth to age 5: $350/month for the first child (universal), $250 for the second and $150 for third-plus children with the additional-child amounts tapered above $150,000 household income; funds are paid by default to the mother but can be split 50/50 at either parent's request; no use restrictions; financed by consolidating existing child-related tax credits and a 1% surcharge on incomes over $500,000. Merit: maximizes family choice and reduces early-child poverty; Tradeoff: large fiscal cost and does not directly expand childcare supply.

Extended Paid Parental Leave with Caregiver Allowance: Provide 12 months paid leave per child at 80% wage replacement up to £35,000/year, with 3 months reserved for each parent; offer an optional £400/month Caregiver Allowance for up to 12 additional months if a parent stays home full‑time; after this period, offer means‑tested childcare vouchers for work return; Funded by a 0.5% increase in employer NICs and general taxation; Trade-off: high fiscal cost and potential short‑term labour supply reduction.

National Childcare Price Cap and Quality Uplift: Set a maximum hourly fee (e.g., £6/hour for under‑3s, £5/hour for ages 3–4), with a per‑child government top‑up to providers to meet true costs; require Level 3 qualifications for all room leads within 3 years and 20 hours/year CPD for all staff; create a Childcare Pricing Regulator to enforce caps and prevent provider gaming; Risk: underfunded caps could trigger provider exits, so the top‑up must track wages and rents.

Universal Free Childcare Guarantee from birth to school start: 15 hours/week free from birth–6 months and 30 hours/week free from 6 months–school entry, delivered via a public option and accredited private providers; providers must meet a national wage floor and training standards; funded by a 1% employer payroll levy and a 2% surtax on personal incomes over £150,000; government will add 200,000 places over three years with a placement-right within 12 weeks of application. Merit: removes cost barriers and boosts labor supply; Cost: requires new tax revenue and rapid workforce expansion.

Infant Care Choice Allowance with Time-Limited Universal Hours: for 0–12 months, all families receive 10 hours/week of free licensed care or home-visiting support; families under 1.25× median income may opt instead for a monthly cash allowance to provide care at home; from 12–36 months, support shifts to sliding-scale vouchers rather than universal free hours; includes pension credits for primary caregivers and return-to-work grants for employers offering flexible schedules. Merit: accommodates differing parental needs and reduces program cost; Cost/tradeoff: smaller universal component may limit immediate full-time returns to work and requires oversight to prevent misuse.
